title: Which statements about pockets are true?
description: Two dot plots of pockets on clothing, for boys and for girls, are read for the gap between values, the median, the mean and the maximum. Each of four statements is tested with the one measure it names.
teaching_notes: One idea: each statement names one measure, so find that measure for both groups and compare. Watch for children who judge variation by the number of dots instead of the gap between values.

video_script.why: The child can find a mean and a maximum and now tests claims that use them.
video_script.substitution: Each statement needs only one measure, found for both groups.
video_script.anchor: Two dot plots of the number of pockets on clothing, one for a group of boys and one for a group of girls, beside four statements
video_script.payoff_line: Only the statement about medians is true.

final_answer.spoken: only the statement about medians is true

maths_rules: boys' gap 6 - 3 = 3; girls' gap 6 - 0 = 6: girls vary more, so the first statement is false
boys' median (5 + 5) ÷ 2 = 5; girls' median is the 7th value, 4: the second statement is true
boys' mean 56 ÷ 12 ≈ 4.67; girls' mean 45 ÷ 13 ≈ 3.46: the third statement is false
both maximums are 6: the fourth statement is false
video_script.design: One idea: one measure per statement. The two dot plots stay in the anchor and the four statement cards sit on the stage.
open_questions: The dot-plot values come from the worklist (the plots are images in the book) and could not be checked against the book text.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; two dot plots of pockets on clothing, one for boys and one for girls, beside four statement cards

marks.m1: the title card From your book appears

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two dot plots show the number of pockets on clothing, one for boys and one for girls.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Four statements compare the two groups.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Which statements are true?

beats.on_screen: the dot plots and the four statements stay on the board

marks.m1: Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a sorted list under each dot plot; the middle value marked median; the greatest value marked maximum

marks.m1: each dot plot turns into a sorted list
marks.m2: the middle value of a list is marked median
marks.m3: the greatest value is marked maximum
marks.m4: the hint line the same way as the book's example glows

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Read each dot plot as a sorted list of values.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The middle value of a sorted list is called the median.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The greatest value is called the maximum.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>We solve it the same way as the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, of twelve boys, one has three pockets, four have four, five have five, two have six.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Of thirteen girls, one has none, one has two, and four have three. Five have four, one has five, and one has six.

beats.on_screen: To find: which of the four statements are true

marks.m1: the question is written under the lists

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find which of the four statements are true.

beats.on_screen: gap = greatest - least: boys 6 - 3 = 3; girls 6 - 0 = 6; maximum of both groups = 6

marks.m3: the first and the fourth cards get False

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, find the gap between the greatest and the least value. This shows how much the data varies.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>For the boys, six take away three is three. For the girls, six take away zero is six.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The girls vary more, so the first statement is false. Both maximums are six, so the fourth is false too.

beats.on_screen: boys: 6th and 7th values 5 and 5, median 5; girls: 7th value 4, median 4

marks.m1: the sixth and seventh boys' values glow
marks.m3: the seventh girls' value glows and 4 appears

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, find the median of each group. With twelve boys, the median lies between the sixth and seventh values.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Both are five, so the boys' median is five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>With thirteen girls, the seventh value is the middle one. It is four, so the girls' median is four.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The boys' median is more, so the second statement is true.

beats.on_screen: mean = total ÷ number of values: boys (3 + 4×4 + 5×5 + 2×6) ÷ 12 = 56 ÷ 12 ≈ 4.67; girls 45 ÷ 13 ≈ 3.46

marks.m1: total ÷ number of values is written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, find the mean of each group. It is the total divided by the number of values.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Adding all twelve boys' values gives fifty six. Fifty six divided by twelve is about four point six seven.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The girls' values add up to forty five. Forty five divided by thirteen is about three point four six.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The girls' mean is smaller, so the third statement is false.

beats.on_screen: check: gaps 3 and 6; medians 5 and 4; means 4.67 and 3.46; maximums 6 and 6

marks.m1: the four pairs of numbers are written beside the four cards
marks.m2: each card is matched with its pair

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, check the answer. Put the numbers back beside each statement.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Three statements fail against their numbers and one holds.

beats.on_screen: Answer: only (b) is true; boys' median 5 is more than girls' median 4
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Only the statement about medians is true.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The boys' median is five, and the girls' median is four.
